pages.x: Nigeria, free from Britain since 1960, joined over 250 peoples under one flag, above all the Hausa and Fulani of the north, the Yoruba of the west and the Igbo of the east. In January 1966 a coup led mostly by Igbo officers killed the prime minister and other leaders, and in July northern officers struck back.

In the north, mobs and soldiers turned on Igbo people living there. In 1966 thousands, perhaps tens of thousands, were murdered, and more than a million fled back to the east. Its military governor, Colonel Odumegwu Ojukwu, said his people were no longer safe in Nigeria.
pages.of: Igbo killed in the north in 1966

pages.x: A deal made at talks in Ghana fell apart, and on 30 May 1967 Ojukwu declared the Eastern Region the independent Republic of Biafra, named after the bay off its coast. Much of Nigeria's oil lay there. Nigeria's young leader, Yakubu Gowon, called it rebellion, and in July sent in troops for what he expected to be a short police action.

In August a Biafran column crossed the Niger and swept deep into the west, alarming Lagos, before it was driven back. Then the federal army, far bigger and armed by Britain and the Soviet Union, slowly closed in. It took Enugu, the Biafran capital, in October 1967, and Port Harcourt, its port, in May 1968.

With its ports and roads cut off, the Biafran enclave shrank, packed with refugees, and food ran out. Photographs of starving children, their bellies swollen by hunger, went around the world. At the worst, aid workers said, thousands were dying every day.
pages.of: Biafrans dead, most of them from hunger

pages.x: Church charities flew food in by night, without lights, to a stretch of road at Uli that served as Biafra's airport, dodging federal bombers. French doctors who worked in Biafra went on to found Doctors Without Borders, to speak out about suffering that others kept quiet about.

In January 1970 federal troops split the enclave and overran Uli. Ojukwu flew into exile, and Biafra surrendered on 15 January. Gowon declared that there would be no victor and no vanquished, and the massacre many had feared did not come. But many Igbo lost their savings and their property.

Nigeria stayed one country, but the war left deep scars, and Igbo grievances have never fully healed. Chinua Achebe, Biafra's most famous writer, wrote about it to the end of his life, and Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie told its story to a new generation in her novel Half of a Yellow Sun.
pts: The east broke away as Biafra in 1967
